newsitem.title: UK: WITNESS SAYS WANTED TO CRUSH FOOTBALLER GROBBELAAR.
newsitem.headline: WITNESS SAYS WANTED TO CRUSH FOOTBALLER GROBBELAAR.

text.p: The main witness in Britain's soccer match-rigging trial on Tuesday admitted he wanted to make as much money as possible from the case while crushing former Liverpool goalkeeper Bruce Grobbelaar.
Chris Vincent, a former friend and business partner of Grobbelaar, covertly recorded the goalkeeper as, according to the prosecution, he admitted rigging games for a Far Eastern betting syndicate.

Under questioning from Grobbelaar's lawyer Rodney Klevan, Vincent said he wanted revenge after a company he formed to market safari holidays in Zimbabwe collapsed when Grobbelaar, who had invested 65,000 pounds ($108,000) in it, pulled out.
"Therefore, if you could kill two birds with one stone, you would gain financially and destroy Grobbelaar?" asked Klevan.
"Correct, sir," answered Vincent.
"You thought that what he had done was so wicked that he had to be destroyed?" Klevan asked later.
"Yes," said Vincent, who admitted that since 1984 he had been director of four companies in southern Africa and Britain, all of which had failed.
Grobbelaar and three others are charged with match-fixing and Vincent's secret tapes, covertly recorded by a tabloid newspaper, are a crucial part of the evidence.

Vincent said Grobbelaar told him that co-defendant and former Wimbledon striker John Fashanu -- accused of being a middleman for the syndicate -- had made a surprise move to Aston Villa in 1994 because match-fixing had become too risky.

Also on trial are Malaysian businessman Heng Suan Lim, accused of being a middleman for the syndicate, and former Wimbledon goalkeeper Hans Segers, accused with Lim and Fashanu of taking part in a separate bid to fix matches.
All four defendants have pleaded not guilty.
On one of the tapes Grobbelaar was seen taking 2,000 pounds in cash which Vincent said he told the goalkeeper had come from another betting syndicate that wanted him to rig matches.
Vincent says he told Grobbelaar the mythical syndicate would pay him 2,000 pounds every fortnight to predict the results of games, plus a further 100,000 pounds for rigging each match.
Klevan portrayed Vincent as a parasite who had lived well off Grobbelaar's money but decided to strike back when the keeper stopped putting funds into the safari company.
"Your God is money, isn't it?" asked Klevan. "No sir," replied Vincent, who like Grobbelaar is from Zimbabwe.
"If this safari plan had succeeded, you would have reaped the rewards, but none of the liabilities had it failed, isn't that fair?" asked Klevan.
"Yes," said Vincent, who has signed a 76,000-pound book deal as well as negotiating film rights.
"Without the money from this you are a man without money, aren't you?" asked Klevan. "Yes, sir," replied Vincent.
Grobbelaar invested 5,000 pounds in the Mondoro safari company a day after the two men first met in July 1992, money which Vincent used to pay off his rent and other debts.
He admitted he had invested little of his own money in the four failed companies, made no effort to pay off his creditors and did not tell Grobbelaar about the bankruptcies.
"When Mondoro folded, you turned like a viper on Grobbelaar, didn't you, when he had been the best of friends?" asked Klevan. "Yes," replied Vincent.
The prosecution says Grobbelaar tried to rig four games for the syndicate while playing for Liverpool and Southampton.
Vincent says he was with Grobbelaar when he received 40,000 pounds in late 1993 for throwing an away match against Newcastle when still playing for Liverpool. ($1=.6021 Pound)
